newsitem.title: HAITI: Second day of rioting spreads in Haitian capital.
newsitem.headline: Second day of rioting spreads in Haitian capital.

text.p: Angry mobs burned cars and tires and exchanged gunfire with police in the streets of the Haitian capital on Friday as student demonstrations flared into a second day of general rioting.
Businesses closed and downtown Port-au-Prince residents fled as the rioters hurled rocks at vehicles and people.

"I can't stay at my home because they are tearing apart everything in the neighbourhood," said one panicked resident lugging a suitcase through a crowd of rioters. Half of the cars leaving the downtown area had broken windscreens.
About 80 police were deployed to restore order, but by noon smaller riots were springing up in other areas of the city, including the downtown slum of La Saline.
"People are just exploding," said a police officer who was limping after being hit in the foot with a rock at a barricade of burning tires in La Saline.

U.S. soldiers, who are only supposed to be doing infrastructure and humanitarian work in Haiti, were on the streets during the riots along with U.N. peacekeepers and Haitian National Police units, police chief Lionel Trecil told Reuters.

Hospital officials said they treated several wounded rioters. Journalists were threatened by rioters and at least one, Radio Ibo reporter Rodner Jean-Baptiste, was beaten by rioters who stole his two-way radio.

Five people were seriously injured in Thursday's riots. A police officer was shot six times and killed overnight by unknown attackers not far from his home. An off-duty officer who was with him was shot in the foot.
Trecil said the shooting did not take place during the riots, but was the result of "criminals taking advantage of the situation of general disorder."
An employee of the Haitian National Police was also killed on Thursday night, although police officials said they did not know if it could be attributed to the general unrest.
The rioting was triggered by student protests that began after teachers went on strike, closing schools just before final exams, because they have not been paid for 14 months.
Angry student Thursday and began throwing rocks at passers-by. When police moved in hundreds of people began to riot, smashing windscreens and setting the courthouse, vehicles and tires on fire.
By the end of Thursday the rioting had less to do with students than with the population's general frustration.
Groups who are opposed to the government's privatisation plans and are demanding that Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resign took advantage of the demonstrations to take to the streets.
Smarth, interviewed by Haitian Radio Metropole in Chile, said he was working seriously on the teachers' dispute.
"That the children are suffering is a shame. We need to find a way out of this."
Smarth said earlier in the week that this year's Haitian budget, which was recently approved by parliament, does not include money to pay the teachers the amount they are owed.
